title: Unit 7 - Review Title Slide
summary: Title slide for the CS 103 Unit 7 Final Review lecture, taught by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: Unit 7 - Review. Course: CS 103. Instructor: Mark Redekopp. This unit provides a comprehensive final review covering classes, operator overloading, copy semantics, inheritance, polymorphism, data structure efficiency, recursion tracing, and programming exercises.
notes_text: This review unit consolidates all major topics from the CS 103 course in preparation for the final exam. Students should use this as a study guide to identify areas needing further review.

title: Classes Review Section
summary: Section divider introducing the classes review portion of the final review.
main_text: This section reviews key concepts related to C++ classes including const function arguments, const member functions, constructor initialization lists, constructor order, friend functions, and friend classes.
notes_text: Classes are a foundational topic in CS 103. Understanding access control, const correctness, and constructor mechanics is essential for the final exam.

title: Review [1] - Const Function Arguments and Const Member Functions
summary: Reviews const function arguments that prevent modification, and const member functions that guarantee no data member changes.
main_text: Const function arguments: Will this code compile? Indicate what will be printed (assuming it compiles). Code example: void f1(const vector<int>& x) { x.push_back(103); x.push_back(104); }. void f2(string& y) { y = 'Bye'; }. int main() { vector<int> a; string b = 'Hi'; f1(a); f2(b); cout << b.size() << endl; return 0; }. Const Member Functions: What does the highlighted const keyword imply in the code? class Item { int val; public: void foo(); int bar() const; }; void Item::foo() { val = 5; }. int Item::bar() const { return val+1; }. void f1(const Item& arg) { int x = arg.bar(); // fine. arg.foo(); // Compiler Error! }
notes_text: The const keyword on function parameters prevents modification of the argument inside the function. Using const references is efficient (avoids copying) while protecting the original data. A const member function promises not to modify any data members of the object, which is why it can be called on const references but non-const member functions cannot.

title: Review [2] - Constructor Initialization Lists and Constructor Order
summary: Reviews constructor initialization lists for efficient member initialization and the order in which constructors are called for composed objects.
main_text: Constructor Initialization Lists: What is the most efficient means to initialize the vals member to an initial array size of 20 and s to a user-defined argument? class Thing { public: Thing(const std::string& s_init); private: vector<int> vals; string s; }; Thing::Thing(const std::string& s_init) { // is this the most efficient way? vals.resize(20); s = s_init; }. Constructor Order: What is printed by the code below? class ABC { public: ABC() { cout << 'ABC' << endl; } }; class DEF { public: DEF() { cout << 'DEF' << endl; } }; class XYZ { ABC m1; DEF m2; public: XYZ() { cout << 'XYZ' << endl; } }; int main() { XYZ x1; return 0; }
notes_text: Constructor initialization lists are more efficient than assignment in the constructor body because they initialize members directly rather than default-constructing then reassigning. For the constructor order question, member objects are constructed in the order they are declared in the class, before the containing class constructor body executes.

title: Review [3] - Friend Functions and Friend Classes
summary: Reviews the friend keyword for granting external functions access to private members, and how classes can grant friend access to other classes.
main_text: Friend Functions: What does the highlighted friend keyword imply in the code? What would break if we remove friend? class Complex { public: Complex(); Complex(double r, double i); friend Complex operator+(const int&, const Complex&); private: double real, imag; }; Complex operator+(const int& lhs, const Complex &rhs) { Complex temp; temp.real = lhs + rhs.real; temp.imag = rhs.imag; return temp; }. Friend Classes: Can DEF::clear() access obj.x? If not, how can class ABC grant access to DEF? class ABC { int x; // data member public: ... }; class DEF { public: void clear(ABC& obj) { obj.x = 0; } };
notes_text: The friend keyword allows a non-member function to access private members of a class. This is commonly needed for operator overloads where the left operand is not a class instance. Without friend, the operator+ function could not access real and imag. For friend classes, ABC must declare DEF as a friend to grant access. A class controls who its friends are, not the other way around.

title: Classes Solutions Section
summary: Section divider marking the beginning of solutions for the classes review questions.
main_text: This section provides solutions to the classes review questions covering const arguments, const member functions, constructor initialization lists, constructor order, friend functions, and friend classes.
notes_text: Students should attempt the review questions before looking at solutions to maximize learning benefit.

title: Review [1] Solution - Const Arguments and Const Member Functions
summary: Solution: f1 will not compile due to modifying a const reference. b.size() would print 3. Const member functions cannot modify data members.
main_text: Const function arguments solution: Will this code compile? No, modification of x in f1(). The function f1 takes a const vector<int>& x, so calling x.push_back() tries to modify a const reference, causing a compiler error. Indicate what will be printed (assuming it compiles): b.size() will be 3, because f2 changes b from 'Hi' to 'Bye' via the non-const reference, and 'Bye' has 3 characters. Const Member Functions solution: The const keyword on bar() implies that no data members can be modified nor non-const member functions called. In f1(const Item& arg), calling arg.bar() is fine because bar() is const, but calling arg.foo() causes a Compiler Error because foo() is not const and could modify the object.
notes_text: Key takeaway: const references prevent any modification. Const member functions provide a guarantee that the function will not change the object state. Only const member functions can be called on const references or const objects. This is a fundamental part of C++ const correctness.

title: Review [2] Solution - Initialization Lists and Constructor Order
summary: Solution: Use initialization list syntax : vals(20), s(s_init). Constructor order prints ABC, DEF, XYZ based on member declaration order.
main_text: Constructor Initialization Lists solution: The most efficient way is to use an initialization list: Thing::Thing(const std::string& s_init) : vals(20), s(s_init) { }. This directly initializes vals with size 20 and s with s_init, avoiding default construction followed by reassignment. Constructor Order solution: The output is ABC, DEF, XYZ. When XYZ x1 is created: first member m1 (type ABC) is constructed, printing 'ABC'. Then member m2 (type DEF) is constructed, printing 'DEF'. Finally the XYZ constructor body runs, printing 'XYZ'. Members are always constructed in declaration order, regardless of the order in initialization lists.
notes_text: Initialization lists are preferred over assignment in the constructor body because they avoid the overhead of default construction plus assignment. For constructor order, remember that members are constructed in the order they are declared in the class definition, not the order they appear in the initialization list. This is important to avoid subtle bugs.

title: Review [3] Solution - Friend Functions and Friend Classes
summary: Solution: friend allows operator+ to access private members. Without it, rhs.real/rhs.imag inaccessible. DEF needs friend declaration from ABC.
main_text: Friend Functions solution: The friend keyword means that function can access Complex private members. What would break if we remove friend? Can't access rhs.real/rhs.imag since they are private members of Complex. The operator+ function needs direct access to the private real and imag data members to perform the addition. Friend Classes solution: Can DEF::clear() access obj.x? No, because x is private to ABC. How can class ABC grant access to DEF? Add friend definition. ABC must include 'friend class DEF;' in its class definition to grant DEF access to its private members.
notes_text: The friend mechanism is C++'s controlled way of breaking encapsulation when needed. The key principle is that friendship is granted by the class being accessed (ABC declares DEF as friend), not claimed by the accessing class. Friendship is not inherited, not transitive, and not reciprocal.

title: Operator Overloading Review Section
summary: Section divider introducing the operator overloading review portion.
main_text: This section reviews operator overloading concepts including member vs non-member operator functions, argument counts, return types, and operator chaining.
notes_text: Operator overloading allows user-defined types to work with standard operators like +, ==, <<, etc. Understanding when to use member vs non-member functions and correct return types is critical.

title: Operator Overloading Review - Member vs Non-member and Arguments
summary: Reviews when to use member vs non-member operator overloads and how many arguments each type requires for binary and unary operators.
main_text: Member or Non-member? How do you decide if you can make the operator overload function a member function of the class? When do you have to use a non-member operator function? Example: class BigInt { ... }; int main() { BigInt x, y, z; x = y + 5; }. Arguments: For member function operator overloads, how many input arguments are needed for operator+? For operator!? Code: class BigInt { ___ operator+( ); ___ operator!( ); }; int main() { BigInt w, x, y, z; w = x + y; bool flag = !w; }
notes_text: You can make an operator a member function when the left-hand operand is an instance of the class. If the left operand is NOT an instance (e.g., int + BigInt), you must use a non-member function. For member functions, the left operand is implicitly 'this', so binary operators need only 1 explicit argument and unary operators need 0.

title: Operator Overloading Review - Return Types and Chaining
summary: Reviews appropriate return types for operator overloads (BigInt for +, bool for ==) and how chaining works without needing multi-input overloads.
main_text: Return types: For class BigInt which models an arbitrary precision integer, what should the return type be for: Operator+ and Operator==? Code: class BigInt { public: ___ operator+(const BigInt&); ___ operator==(const BigInt&); }; int main() { BigInt w, x, y, z; w = x + y; }. Chaining: Do we need operator overload functions with 2-, 3-, 4-inputs, etc. to handle various use cases? Code: int main() { BigInt w, x, y, z; w = x + y + z; cout << w << ' is a bigint!' << endl; }
notes_text: Operator+ should return BigInt by value (a new object representing the sum). Operator== should return bool. Chaining (x + y + z) works because x + y returns a BigInt temporary, then that temporary + z returns another BigInt. No multi-argument overloads are needed because chaining evaluates left-to-right.

title: Operator Overloading Solution Section
summary: Section divider marking the beginning of solutions for operator overloading review questions.
main_text: This section provides solutions to the operator overloading review questions.
notes_text: Solutions cover member vs non-member decisions, argument counts, return types, and chaining behavior.

title: Operator Overloading Solution - Member vs Non-member and Arguments
summary: Solution: Use member when left operand is class instance. Non-member when left operand is different type. operator+ needs 1 arg, operator! needs 0.
main_text: Member or Non-member solution: How do you decide if you can make the operator overload function a member function of the class? If the left-hand side operand is a class instance, you can use a member function. When do you have to use a non-member operator function? If the left operand of an operator is NOT an instance of the class, you cannot use a member function. Arguments solution: For member function operator overloads, how many input arguments are needed for operator+? Only 1, the left side operand is 'this'. For operator!? None, the left side operand is 'this'. Code: class BigInt { ___ operator+(const BigInt& rhs); ___ operator!(); };
notes_text: The implicit 'this' pointer serves as the left operand for member operator functions. This is why binary operators need n-1 explicit parameters (1 for binary, 0 for unary). For x + y, x becomes 'this' and y is the explicit parameter. For !w, w becomes 'this' with no explicit parameters.

title: Operator Overloading Solution - Return Types and Chaining
summary: Solution: operator+ returns BigInt (by value), operator== returns bool. Chaining works via left-to-right evaluation: x.operator+(y).operator+(z).
main_text: Return types solution: Operator+: BigInt (by value). Operator==: bool. Code: class BigInt { public: BigInt operator+(const BigInt&); bool operator==(const BigInt&); }; Chaining solution: Do we need operator overload functions with 2-, 3-, 4-inputs? No, this is why the return type should be BigInt to allow for chaining: x.operator+(y).operator+(z), etc. The expression w = x + y + z is evaluated as w = (x + y) + z. First x + y produces a temporary BigInt, then that temporary + z produces another BigInt assigned to w.
notes_text: The return type of operator+ must be BigInt (not void or bool) specifically to enable chaining. If operator+ returned void, you could not write x + y + z. Similarly, operator<< for ostream must return ostream& to allow cout << a << b << c chaining.

title: Copy Review Section
summary: Section divider introducing the copy semantics review covering copy constructors, assignment operators, and the Rule of 3.
main_text: This section reviews copy semantics in C++ including copy constructor prototypes, distinguishing copy constructor calls from assignment operator calls, default copy behavior (shallow copies), the Rule of 3, and assignment operator considerations.
notes_text: Copy semantics are critical for classes that manage dynamic memory. Incorrect copy behavior leads to bugs like double-free errors, dangling pointers, and memory leaks.

title: Copy Review [1] - Copy Constructor Prototype
summary: Reviews the three possible copy constructor prototypes and asks which is correct for creating c3 as a copy of c1.
main_text: What is the correct prototype for the copy constructor call when c3 is created in the code to the right? Three options presented: Complex(Complex); Complex(Complex &); Complex(const Complex &). Code: class Complex { public: Complex(); Complex(double r, double i); // What constructor definition do I need for c3's declaration below private: double real, imag; }; int main() { Complex c1(2,3), c2(4,5); Complex c3(c1); }
notes_text: This question tests understanding of copy constructor signature requirements. The correct answer involves understanding why pass-by-value won't work (infinite recursion), why non-const reference is possible but not ideal, and why const reference is the best practice.

title: Copy Review [2] - Which Function and Default Versions
summary: Reviews distinguishing copy constructor calls from assignment operator calls, and asks what kind of copy default versions perform.
main_text: Which function? For each of the following, identify whether the copy constructor is called or the assignment operator: Complex c1; Complex c2 = c1; (which one?). Complex c1; Complex c2(c1); (which one?). Complex c1, c2; c2 = c1; (which one?). Default Versions: What kind of copy does the default copy constructor and assignment operator perform? Code: class MyArray { ... private: int* data; // ptr to dynamic array size_t len; };
notes_text: The key distinction is: if a new object is being created, it's the copy constructor. If an existing object is being assigned to, it's the assignment operator. 'Complex c2 = c1' looks like assignment but is actually copy construction because c2 is being created. The default versions perform shallow copies, which is problematic for classes with pointers to dynamic memory.

title: Copy Review [3] - Rule of 3 and Assignment Operator
summary: Reviews the Rule of 3 and special considerations for the assignment operator including self-assignment and cleanup of old data.
main_text: State the Rule of 3: (fill in the blank exercise). Assignment Operator: What extra considerations does the assignment operator need to handle vs. the copy constructor? What should operator= return? Code: class MyArray { private: int* data; // ptr to dynamic array }; MyArray& operator=(const MyArray& other) { (implementation left blank for students to fill in) }
notes_text: The Rule of 3 states that if a class needs any one of destructor, copy constructor, or assignment operator, it very likely needs all three. The assignment operator has extra considerations beyond the copy constructor: it must handle self-assignment (a = a) and clean up existing data before copying new data. It should return *this (by reference) to support chaining.

title: Copy Solutions Section
summary: Section divider marking the beginning of solutions for copy review questions.
main_text: This section provides solutions to the copy review questions covering copy constructor prototypes, copy constructor vs assignment operator identification, default copy behavior, and the Rule of 3.
notes_text: Solutions clarify the distinction between copy construction and assignment, explain shallow vs deep copy, and detail the Rule of 3.

title: Copy Solution [1] - Copy Constructor Prototype Answer
summary: Solution: Complex(Complex) causes infinite recursion, Complex(Complex&) is possible, Complex(const Complex&) is best practice.
main_text: What is the correct prototype for the copy constructor? Complex(Complex); - We will see that this can't be right because passing by value would itself invoke the copy constructor, causing infinite recursion. Complex(Complex &) - Possible, it works. Complex(const Complex &) - Best! Making a copy shouldn't change the input argument, thus 'const'. This is the standard and recommended signature for copy constructors in C++.
notes_text: The pass-by-value option Complex(Complex) would create an infinite loop: to call the copy constructor, you'd need to copy the argument, which calls the copy constructor, which needs to copy the argument, and so on forever. The const reference version is best because it documents the intent that the source object will not be modified during copying, and allows copying from const objects.

title: Copy Solution [2] - Which Function and Default Versions Answer
summary: Solution: First two cases are copy constructor, third is assignment operator. Default versions perform shallow copies.
main_text: Which function? Complex c1; Complex c2 = c1; - copy constructor (c2 is being created). Complex c1; Complex c2(c1); - copy constructor (c2 is being created). Complex c1, c2; c2 = c1; - assignment operator (c2 already exists). Default Versions: What kind of copy does the default copy constructor and assignment operator perform? Shallow Copies! For the MyArray class with int* data and size_t len, a shallow copy copies the pointer value but not the data it points to, meaning both objects share the same dynamic array. This leads to double-free bugs when both objects are destroyed.
notes_text: The critical distinction: if a NEW object is being initialized, it's copy construction. If an EXISTING object receives a new value, it's assignment. The '=' in 'Complex c2 = c1' is initialization syntax, not assignment. Shallow copies are dangerous for classes with pointers to dynamic memory because modifying one object's data affects the other, and destruction causes double-free.

title: Copy Solution [3] - Rule of 3 and Assignment Operator Answer
summary: Solution: Rule of 3 states if any of destructor/copy ctor/operator= is needed, all 3 likely are. operator= must handle self-assignment and cleanup.
main_text: State the Rule of 3: If a class needs to define ANY ONE of the: destructor, copy constructor, or assignment operator, THEN it very likely needs to define ALL 3! Having pointers to dynamically allocated data would generally necessitate deep copies and a destructor to deallocate! Assignment Operator solution: What extra considerations does the assignment operator need to handle vs. the copy constructor? Self assignment and cleaning up old data. Unlike the copy constructor which starts with an uninitialized object, the assignment operator must first deallocate any existing resources before copying new ones, and must check for self-assignment (a = a) to avoid destroying data before copying it. What should operator= return? *this (which is of type Obj&) to support chaining like a = b = c.
notes_text: The Rule of 3 is one of the most important design rules in C++. If a class manages resources (dynamic memory, file handles, etc.), all three special functions must be properly implemented. The assignment operator is more complex than the copy constructor because it must clean up the existing state of the left-hand object before copying from the right-hand object, while also handling the edge case of self-assignment.

title: Inheritance Review Questions Section
summary: Section divider introducing the inheritance review questions.
main_text: This section reviews inheritance concepts including member access through inheritance, public vs private inheritance, access specifiers (public, protected, private), and the is-a vs has-a relationships.
notes_text: Inheritance is a core object-oriented programming concept. Understanding access control through inheritance hierarchies is essential for designing class hierarchies correctly.

title: Inheritance Review 1 - Member Access and Private Inheritance
summary: Reviews whether Student objects have and can access inherited private members, and the effect of private inheritance.
main_text: T/F: A student object has a name_ and id_ member. T/F: Code from the Student class can access name_ and id_. What could you change to flip the T/F answer? What would change if Student inherited Person through private inheritance? Code: class Person { public: Person(string n, int ident); string get_name(); int get_id(); private: string name_; int id_; }; class Student : public Person { public: Student(string n, int ident, int mjr); int get_major(); double get_gpa(); void set_gpa(double new_gpa); private: int major_; double gpa_; }; int main() { Student s1('Amanda', 12345, 1); cout << s1.get_name() << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: A Student object DOES have name_ and id_ members (inherited from Person), so the first statement is True. However, Student code CANNOT directly access name_ and id_ because they are private to Person, so the second statement is False. To flip the answer, change Person's access specifier to protected or public. With private inheritance, external code could not call inherited public methods like get_name().

title: Inheritance Review 2 - Relationships and Protected Access
summary: Fill-in-the-blank review on is-a vs has-a relationships and protected access making members accessible to derived classes.
main_text: Inheritance defines an _______ relationship between classes. Composition defines a _________ relationship between two objects. Protected access makes members accessible to ____________ but still not to _________________. These three fill-in-the-blank questions test fundamental OOP terminology and access control concepts.
notes_text: Inheritance models is-a relationships (a Student is-a Person). Composition models has-a relationships (a Car has-a Engine). Protected access is the middle ground between public and private: it allows derived classes to access members directly while still hiding them from external code. These are core OOP design principles.

title: Inheritance Solutions Section
summary: Section divider marking the beginning of solutions for inheritance review questions.
main_text: This section provides solutions to the inheritance review questions.
notes_text: Solutions cover member access through inheritance, the effect of changing access specifiers, private inheritance behavior, and relationship terminology.

title: Inheritance Review 1 Solution
summary: Solution: Student has name_ and id_ (True). Student cannot access them directly (False). Change to protected/public to flip. Private inheritance hides inherited public methods from external code.
main_text: T/F: A student object has a name_ and id_ member - True. Student inherits all members from Person, including name_ and id_. T/F: Code from the Student class can access name_ and id_ - False. Because name_ and id_ are private in Person, even derived classes cannot access them directly. What could you change to flip the T/F answer? Changing Person's access specifier to protected or public. Regardless of how Student inherits, name_ and id_ will be private to the Student class (meaning Student code cannot access them directly). What would change if Student inherited Person through private inheritance? External clients (like main) would not be able to access the inherited members (from Person) of a Student object. Methods like get_name() would become private in Student.
notes_text: This is a subtle but important distinction: inheritance determines what exists in the derived class, but the base class access specifier determines what the derived class code can directly access. Private members of the base are NEVER directly accessible to derived classes regardless of inheritance type. Protected and public inheritance differ in how inherited public/protected members appear to external code.

title: Inheritance Review 2 Solution
summary: Solution: Inheritance defines is-a relationship. Composition defines has-a relationship. Protected makes members accessible to derived/child classes but not external/3rd-party clients.
main_text: Inheritance defines an is-a relationship between classes (e.g., a Student is-a Person). Composition defines a has-a relationship between two objects (e.g., a Car has-a Engine). Protected access makes members accessible to derived/child class but still not to external/3rd-party clients. Protected is the ideal access level for base class members that derived classes need to access directly, while still maintaining encapsulation from external code.
notes_text: These three concepts form the foundation of OOP design. The is-a test helps determine whether inheritance is appropriate: if you can naturally say 'X is-a Y', inheritance makes sense. If the relationship is 'X has-a Y', composition is more appropriate. Protected access bridges the gap between fully open (public) and fully closed (private) for inheritance hierarchies.

title: Polymorphism Review Questions Section
summary: Section divider introducing the polymorphism review questions covering virtual functions, static vs dynamic binding, and abstract classes.
main_text: This section reviews polymorphism concepts including virtual functions, static vs dynamic binding, pure virtual functions, abstract classes, and virtual destructors.
notes_text: Polymorphism allows code to work with objects of different types through a common interface. Understanding which function is called (static vs dynamic binding) based on whether virtual is used is a critical exam topic.

title: Polymorphism Review Questions 1 - Virtual Functions and Binding
summary: Reviews which member functions are called through a base pointer depending on whether virtual is used, introducing static vs dynamic binding.
main_text: As we call processPerson(&p) what member functions will be called (e.g. Person::print_info, CSStudent::useComputer, etc.)? As we call processPerson(&s)? As we call processPerson(&cs)? We use the terms static and dynamic binding when referring to which function will be called when virtual is NOT or IS present. Code: class Person { public: virtual void print_info() const; // name, ID void useComputer(); // stream a show string name; int id; }; class Student : public Person { public: void print_info() const; // print major void useComputer(); // write a paper int major; double gpa; }; class CSStudent : public Student { public: void print_info() const; // print OH queue pos void useComputer(); // fight with Docker }; void processPerson(Person* p) { p->print_info(); p->useComputer(); }
notes_text: Since print_info() is declared virtual in Person, it uses dynamic binding (calls the function matching the actual object type). Since useComputer() is NOT virtual, it uses static binding (calls the function matching the pointer type, which is always Person*). This is the fundamental difference between static and dynamic binding.

title: Polymorphism Review Questions 2 - Pure Virtual and Abstract Classes
summary: Reviews pure virtual functions (=0), abstract classes, inherited implementations, and when to use virtual destructors.
main_text: What does '=0;' mean in the declarations to the right? What do we call a class with 1 or more of these kind of declarations? Is it okay that Student doesn't provide a useComputer() implementation? Can we declare Person objects? Can we declare pointers or references to Person objects? When should a class have a virtual destructor? Code: class Person { public: virtual void print_info() const = 0; virtual void useComputer(); // stream a show string name; int id; }; class Student : public Person { public: void print_info() const; // print major int major; double gpa; }; class CSStudent : public Student { public: void print_info() const; // print OH queue pos void useComputer(); // fight with Docker }; void printPerson(Person* p) { p->print_info(); } void compute(Person& p) { p.useComputer(); }
notes_text: =0 declares a pure virtual function, meaning no implementation is provided in the base class and derived classes MUST override it. A class with one or more pure virtual functions is called an abstract class. You cannot create instances of abstract classes, but you CAN declare pointers and references to them (which is essential for polymorphism). Student doesn't need its own useComputer() because it inherits Person's implementation. Virtual destructors should be used when a class has any virtual functions.

title: Polymorphism Solutions Section
summary: Section divider marking the beginning of solutions for polymorphism review questions.
main_text: This section provides solutions to the polymorphism review questions.
notes_text: Solutions explain static vs dynamic binding, which functions are called through base pointers, and abstract class rules.

title: Polymorphism Solution 1 - Which Functions Are Called
summary: Solution: Virtual print_info uses dynamic binding (calls actual type's version). Non-virtual useComputer uses static binding (always Person's version).
main_text: As we call processPerson(&p): Person::print_info() / Person::useComputer(). Both the pointer type and actual object type are Person. As we call processPerson(&s): Student::print_info() / Person::useComputer(). print_info() is virtual so it calls Student's version (dynamic binding based on actual object type). useComputer() is not virtual so it calls Person's version (static binding based on pointer type). As we call processPerson(&cs): CSStudent::print_info() / Person::useComputer(). print_info() is virtual so it calls CSStudent's version. useComputer() is not virtual so Person's version is called. We use the terms static and dynamic binding when referring to which function will be called when virtual is NOT or IS present.
notes_text: This is the most important polymorphism concept. Virtual functions enable dynamic binding where the actual type of the object determines which function runs. Non-virtual functions use static binding where the type of the pointer/reference determines which function runs. Dynamic binding is what makes polymorphism useful - you can process different object types through a common base pointer.

title: Polymorphism Solution 2 - Pure Virtual and Abstract Classes Answers
summary: Solution: =0 means pure virtual function. Class with pure virtuals is abstract. Student inherits useComputer(). Cannot instantiate Person. Can have pointers/references. Virtual destructor when any virtual function exists.
main_text: What does '=0;' mean? Pure virtual function - no implementation provided, derived classes must override. What do we call a class with 1 or more of these? Abstract class. Is it okay that Student doesn't provide a useComputer() implementation? Yes, it inherits Person::useComputer(). Can we declare Person objects? No, Person is abstract (has pure virtual function). Can we declare pointers or references to Person objects? Yes, this is essential for polymorphism. When should a class have a virtual destructor? When at least one other virtual function is declared in the class. This ensures proper cleanup when deleting through base pointers.
notes_text: Abstract classes serve as interfaces that define what derived classes must implement. You cannot create instances of abstract classes, but you CAN use them as pointer/reference types for polymorphism. Virtual destructors are critical: without them, deleting a derived object through a base pointer would only call the base destructor, potentially leaking resources allocated in the derived class.

title: Data Structure Efficiency - Operations Comparison
summary: Table comparing the efficiency of push_back, push_front, get/at, and pop operations across vector, deque, and linked list variants.
main_text: Efficiency comparison table for common data structure operations. Data structures compared: Vector, Deque, Singly-Linked List (w/ head ptr only), Singly-Linked List (w/ head + tail ptr), and Doubly-linked list (w/ head + tail ptr). Operations compared: Push_back(), Push_front(), Get/at(location i), Pop_front(). The table has blank cells for students to fill in the Big-O complexity for each operation on each data structure. Students must reason about which operations require traversal (O(n)) versus direct access (O(1)).

title: Consider This Class - Copy Constructor Exercise
summary: Asks whether a Student class with a char* member needs a custom copy constructor, and to define one if so.
main_text: Does this class need to define a copy constructor? If so, define it. class Student { public: Student(string name, char* mjr) { name_ = name; major = new char[strlen(mjr)+1]; strcpy(major, mjr); } void addScore(int s) { scores.push_back(s); } private: string name_; char* major; vector<int> scores_; };. The class uses 'new' to dynamically allocate memory for the major char array. This means the default shallow copy constructor would only copy the pointer, not the data it points to, leading to both objects sharing the same dynamically allocated memory.
notes_text: Yes, this class needs a custom copy constructor because it has a raw pointer (char* major) to dynamically allocated memory. A shallow copy would copy the pointer address, meaning two Student objects would point to the same char array. When one is destroyed, the other would have a dangling pointer. The copy constructor must allocate new memory and copy the string content (deep copy). Note: string and vector handle their own deep copying, so only major needs special treatment.

title: Polymorphism: As Easy as 1-2-3
summary: Presents a 3-step method for determining which function is called through pointers: check pointer type, find prototype, check if virtual.
main_text: Step 1: Determine what type of pointer/reference is being used to call the function. Step 2: Go to the prototype of the function in the class that matches the type of pointer/reference and ask: 'Is it virtual?' at that level in the hierarchy. Step 3a: If no, execute the function from the class matching the pointer type (static binding). Step 3b: If yes, execute the function from the class matching the type of object being pointed to or referenced (dynamic binding). Code: class Person { public: virtual void print_info() const; void code(); string name; int id; }; class Student : public Person { public: void print_info() const; virtual void code(); virtual void study(); int major; double gpa; }; class CSStudent : public Student { public: void code(); void study(); }; Person *q; Student* t; q = &s; q->print_info(); // calls: ___ q->code(); // calls: ___ q = &cs; q->code(); // calls: ___ t = &cs; t->print_info(); // calls: ___ t->code(); // calls: ___
notes_text: This 3-step method is the definitive approach for determining which function is called in polymorphic code. The key insight is that you must check whether virtual appears in the class matching the POINTER TYPE, not the object type. If virtual is declared at that level, dynamic binding kicks in and the actual object's function is called. If not virtual at that level, the pointer type's function is called regardless of the actual object type.

title: Trace the Output - Vehicle Inheritance Hierarchy
summary: Tracing exercise with Vehicle, Bus, and SchoolBus classes to predict output of virtual and non-virtual function calls through base pointers.
main_text: Code: class Vehicle { public: void drive() { honk(); cout << 'Vehicle::drive' << endl; } void honk() { cout << 'Vehicle::honk' << endl; } virtual void brake() { cout << 'Vehicle::brake' << endl; } }; class Bus : public Vehicle { public: void honk() { cout << 'Bus::honk' << endl; } virtual void brake() { drive(); cout << 'Bus::brake' << endl; } }; class SchoolBus : public Bus { public: virtual void brake() { honk(); cout << 'SchoolBus::brake' << endl; } }; int main() { Vehicle *v1 = new Bus(); v1->brake(); Vehicle *v2 = new SchoolBus(); v2->brake(); v2->drive(); delete v1; delete v2; return 0; } // if destructors printed the class name, what would you see?
notes_text: This is a complex tracing exercise that tests understanding of virtual vs non-virtual dispatch. For v1->brake(): brake() is virtual, actual type is Bus, so Bus::brake() is called. Bus::brake() calls drive(), which calls honk(). Since drive() and honk() are called on 'this' (a Bus object) but are NOT virtual, static binding applies and Vehicle versions are called. For v2->brake(): SchoolBus::brake() is called, which calls honk() - since honk is not virtual and we're in Bus-level context, Vehicle::honk() is called.

title: Recursion Tracing - GCD Function
summary: Recursion tracing exercise for a greatest common divisor function using the Euclidean algorithm with gc(120,88) and gc(36,15).
main_text: int gc(int x, int y) { if(y==0) return x; else return gc(y, x%y); } int main() { cout << gc(120, 88) << endl; cout << gc(36, 15) << endl; }. Students must trace the recursive calls. For gc(120, 88): gc(120,88) -> gc(88, 120%88=32) -> gc(32, 88%32=24) -> gc(24, 32%24=8) -> gc(8, 24%8=0) -> returns 8. For gc(36, 15): gc(36,15) -> gc(15, 36%15=6) -> gc(6, 15%6=3) -> gc(3, 6%3=0) -> returns 3.
notes_text: This function implements the Euclidean algorithm for computing the greatest common divisor (GCD). It is an elegant recursive solution where each call reduces the problem by taking the modulo. The base case is when y==0, at which point x is the GCD. This is a practical example of recursion that students should be able to trace through.

title: Recursion Tracing - Complex m1/m2 Functions
summary: Advanced recursion tracing with m1 and m2 functions using pointer arithmetic and reference parameters to find the maximum element in an array.
main_text: Trace this code: int m1(int* dat, int len) { int temp = -1; m2(dat, len, temp); return temp; }. void m2(int* dat, int len, int& num) { if(len <= 1) { num = *dat; } else if(num == -1) { num = 0; m2(dat+1, len-1, num); num += *dat; } else { m2(dat+1, len-1, num); } }. int main() { int data[4] = {3, 6, 2, 9}; cout << m1(data, 4) << endl; // what will be output? }. This exercise combines several concepts: pointer arithmetic (dat+1), reference parameters (int& num), and multiple recursive cases.
notes_text: This is a challenging tracing exercise that combines recursion with pointer arithmetic and reference parameters. Students need to track how dat+1 shifts the array pointer, how len-1 reduces the problem size, and how the reference parameter num is shared across all recursive calls. The function appears to compute something related to summing array elements based on the conditional logic.

title: Programming I - Zip Two Arrays
summary: Programming exercise to write a function that zips two same-sized arrays by alternating elements into a new third array.
main_text: Zip 2 arrays of the same size (alternate taking from each array) into a new 3rd array and return that 3rd array. For example, if array1 = {1, 3, 5} and array2 = {2, 4, 6}, the result would be {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. The function should dynamically allocate a new array of size 2*len, interleave elements from both source arrays, and return the pointer to the new array. Students are given an empty code box to write their solution.
notes_text: This exercise tests dynamic memory allocation, pointer manipulation, and array indexing. The key insight is using 2*i and 2*i+1 as indices in the result array to interleave elements. Students must remember to use 'new' for allocation and that the caller is responsible for eventually deleting the returned array.

title: Programming II - Delete Second Item in Linked List
summary: Programming exercise to write a function that deletes the second item in a singly linked list, with challenge for head and tail pointer variant.
main_text: Given a singly linked list storing values in Item structs (as shown below) and given a head pointer, write a function to delete the 2nd Item in the list (if it exists)? Challenge: How would the code change if there was a head AND tail pointer? struct Item { int val; Item* next; }; void delSecond(Item* head) { (implementation left blank for students) }. Students must handle edge cases: empty list, list with only one element, and the general case of removing the second node.
notes_text: This exercise tests linked list manipulation skills. Key considerations: check if head is NULL, check if head->next is NULL (only one element), save the pointer to the node being deleted, update the next pointer of the first node to skip the second node, then delete the removed node. The tail pointer variant adds the consideration that if the deleted node was the tail, the tail pointer must be updated.

title: Programming III - Change Class Design
summary: Programming exercise to design a Change class with quarters, dimes, pennies that normalizes values and supports operator overloading.
main_text: Make a 'Change' class with data members: quarters, dimes, pennies (no nickels). Provides a constructor to initialize those three values to user-specified arguments but normalizes to use as many quarters as possible, then as many dimes, then as many pennies (i.e. if they pass 1 quarter, 3 dimes, and 11 pennies you'd want to store 2 quarters, 1 dimes, and 6 pennies). Support operator+ and operator== with the requirement to always re-'normalize' after adding. Support an ostream operator that shows the change in the normalized form 'Q:2 D:1 P:6'.
notes_text: This is a comprehensive class design exercise that tests constructor design, normalization logic, operator overloading (member functions for + and ==, friend function for <<), and const correctness. The normalization algorithm converts total cents to the maximum number of quarters, then dimes from the remainder, then pennies.

title: Copy Constructor Solution - Student Class
summary: Solution: Student class needs a copy constructor that deep copies the char* major member using new and strcpy, while using initialization list for other members.
main_text: Does this class need to define a copy constructor? Yes, because it has a char* major that uses dynamic allocation. Solution: Student(const Student& s) : name_(s.name_), scores_(s.scores_) { // or name_ = s.name_; // or scores_ = s.scores_; major_ = new char[strlen(s.major_)+1]; strcpy(major_, s.major_); }. The copy constructor uses an initialization list to efficiently copy name_ and scores_ (which handle their own deep copying as string and vector), then manually performs a deep copy of major_ by allocating new memory and copying the C-string content.
notes_text: This solution demonstrates several important concepts: the initialization list is used for members that can copy themselves correctly (string and vector already perform deep copies). The char* member requires manual deep copy: allocate new memory of the same size (strlen+1 for null terminator), then copy the content with strcpy. Without this custom copy constructor, two Student objects would share the same major_ buffer, leading to double-free bugs.

title: Trace the Output Solution - Vehicle Hierarchy
summary: Solution: v1->brake() outputs Vehicle::honk, Vehicle::drive, Bus::brake. v2->brake() outputs Bus::honk, SchoolBus::brake. v2->drive() outputs Vehicle::honk, Vehicle::drive.
main_text: Solution trace: v1->brake(): brake() is virtual, v1 points to Bus, so Bus::brake() runs. Bus::brake() calls drive(). drive() is non-virtual so Vehicle::drive() runs. Vehicle::drive() calls honk(). honk() is non-virtual so Vehicle::honk() runs. Output: Vehicle::honk, Vehicle::drive, Bus::brake. v2->brake(): brake() is virtual, v2 points to SchoolBus, so SchoolBus::brake() runs. SchoolBus::brake() calls honk(). honk() is non-virtual so Vehicle::honk() runs. Output: Bus::honk (actually Vehicle::honk from within SchoolBus context), SchoolBus::brake. v2->drive(): drive() is non-virtual, pointer is Vehicle*, so Vehicle::drive() runs. Output: Vehicle::honk, Vehicle::drive. If destructors printed class name with virtual destructors, deleting v1 would show Bus then Vehicle, deleting v2 would show SchoolBus then Bus then Vehicle.
notes_text: The critical insight is that non-virtual function calls ALWAYS use the compile-time type (static binding), even when called from within a virtual function. So when Bus::brake() calls drive(), and drive() calls honk(), both use Vehicle's versions because they are non-virtual and the call context is Vehicle (since drive is defined in Vehicle). This is a common source of confusion on exams.

title: Recursion Tracing Solution - GCD Function
summary: Solution: gc(120,88) traces through 5 recursive calls to return 8. gc(36,15) traces through 4 recursive calls to return 3.
main_text: Recursion tracing solution for the GCD function. gc(120, 88): main calls gc(120,88). gc(120,88) calls gc(88, 120%88=32). gc(88,32) calls gc(32, 88%32=24). gc(32,24) calls gc(24, 32%24=8). gc(24,8) calls gc(8, 24%8=0). gc(8,0): y==0, returns x=8. Result: 8. gc(36, 15): main calls gc(36,15). gc(36,15) calls gc(15, 36%15=6). gc(15,6) calls gc(6, 15%6=3). gc(6,3) calls gc(3, 6%3=0). gc(3,0): y==0, returns x=3. Result: 3.
notes_text: The GCD function implements the Euclidean algorithm, one of the oldest known algorithms. Each recursive call reduces the problem by computing x mod y, which is guaranteed to eventually reach 0. The box diagrams show the call chain flowing downward with each call, and the return value (8 or 3) propagating back up through all levels.

title: Recursion Tracing Solution - m1/m2 Functions
summary: Solution trace of m1/m2 functions showing how pointer arithmetic and reference parameter interact to compute the sum of array elements, outputting 12.
main_text: Trace solution for m1/m2 with data[4] = {3, 6, 2, 9}. Call chain: main calls m1(data, 4). m1 sets temp = -1, calls m2(dat, 4, temp). m2(dat,4,ref): num==-1, so num=0, calls m2(dat+1, 3, num). m2(dat+1,3,ref): num==0 (not -1, not <=1), calls m2(dat+2, 2, num). m2(dat+2,2,ref): num==0 (not -1, not <=1), calls m2(dat+3, 1, num). m2(dat+3,1,ref): len<=1, so num = *dat = 9. Returns. Back in m2(dat+2,2,ref): continues, no additional work (else branch). Back in m2(dat+1,3,ref): continues, no additional work. Back in m2(dat,4,ref): num += *dat = 9 + 3 = 12. temp (shared via reference) now holds 12. m1 returns temp = 12. Output: 12.
notes_text: This solution demonstrates how the reference parameter num is shared across all recursive calls. The function first descends to find the last element (num=9 via base case), then on the way back up in the first call, adds the first element (*dat = 3). The middle elements are skipped because only the initial call (where num was -1) has the num += *dat line after the recursive call. The output is 3 + 9 = 12.

images.description: Call chain diagram showing main -> m1(4,ref) -> m2(dat,4,ref) -> m2(dat+1,3,ref) -> m2(dat+2,2,ref) -> m2(dat+3,1,ref), with the shared temp/num variable showing values -1, 0, 9, 12

title: Data Structure Efficiency Solution
summary: Solution table with Big-O complexities for all data structure operations: vectors, deques, singly-linked lists, and doubly-linked lists.
main_text: Efficiency solution table. Vector: Push_back() O(1) w/o resize, O(n) w/ resize. Push_front() O(n). Get/at(location i) O(1). Pop_front() O(n). Deque: Push_back() O(1). Push_front() O(1). Get/at(location i) O(1) if array, O(i) if linked list. Pop_front() O(1). Singly-Linked List (w/ head ptr only): Push_back() O(n). Push_front() O(1). Get/at(location i) O(i). Pop_back() O(n). Singly-Linked List (w/ head + tail ptr): Push_back() O(1). Push_front() O(1). Get/at(location i) O(i). Pop_back() O(n). Doubly-linked list (w/ head + tail ptr): Push_back() O(1). Push_front() O(1). Get/at(location i) O(i). Pop_back() O(1).
notes_text: Key takeaways: Vectors excel at random access O(1) but are slow at front operations O(n). Linked lists excel at front operations O(1) but are slow at random access O(i). Adding a tail pointer makes push_back O(1) for linked lists. Doubly-linked lists with tail pointer achieve O(1) pop_back because they can traverse backward. Deques are optimized for both ends but may sacrifice some random access speed depending on implementation.

title: Programming I Solution - Zip Arrays
summary: Solution for the zip arrays problem using dynamic allocation and interleaved indexing with data[2*i] and data[2*i+1].
main_text: Solution: int* zip(int* src1, int* src2, size_t len) { int* data = new int[2*len]; for(size_t i=0; i < len; i++) { data[2*i] = src1[i]; data[2*i+1] = src2[i]; } return data; }. The function allocates a new array of size 2*len, then iterates through both source arrays simultaneously. For each index i, it places src1[i] at position 2*i (even indices) and src2[i] at position 2*i+1 (odd indices) in the result array. This interleaving pattern produces the desired zip behavior.
notes_text: Key implementation details: 'new int[2*len]' allocates the result array on the heap so it persists after the function returns. The indexing pattern 2*i and 2*i+1 alternates between the two source arrays. The caller is responsible for deleting the returned array to avoid memory leaks. Using size_t for the length parameter is best practice for array sizes.

title: Programming II Solution - Delete Second Item in Linked List
summary: Solution for deleting the second node with both head-only and head+tail pointer variants, including edge case handling.
main_text: With Head Only: struct Item { int val; Item* next; }; void delSecond(Item* head) { if(head == NULL) { return; } else if(head->next == NULL) { return; } else { // head->next cannot be null here Item* toDelete = head->next; head->next = head->next->next; delete toDelete; } }. With Tail Pointer: void delSecond(Item* head) { if(head == NULL) { return; } else if(head->next == NULL) { return; } else { Item* toDelete = head->next; head->next = head->next->next; if(tail == toDelete) { tail = head; } delete toDelete; } }. The tail pointer variant adds a check: if the deleted node was the tail, update tail to point to head (since the list now has only one element).
notes_text: This solution handles three cases: empty list (head==NULL), single element (head->next==NULL), and normal case (at least 2 elements). The key steps are: save a pointer to the node being deleted, redirect the first node's next pointer to skip the second node, then delete the saved pointer. The tail pointer variant must check whether the deleted node was the tail and update accordingly.

title: Programming III - Change Class Requirements (Repeated)
summary: Restatement of the Change class design exercise requirements for reference alongside the solution.
main_text: Make a 'Change' class with data members: quarters, dimes, pennies (no nickels). Provides a constructor to initialize those three values to user-specified arguments but normalizes to use as many quarters as possible, then as many dimes, then as many pennies (i.e. if they pass 1 quarter, 3 dimes, and 11 pennies you'd want to store 2 quarters, 1 dimes, and 6 pennies). Support operator+ and operator== - always re-'normalize' after adding. Support an ostream operator that shows the change in the normalized form 'Q:2 D:1 P:6'.
notes_text: This is the same requirements slide repeated alongside the solution slides for easy reference. The normalization algorithm converts all change to total cents (pennies), then divides by 25 for quarters, takes the remainder and divides by 10 for dimes, and the final remainder is pennies.

title: Programming III Solution - Change Class Declaration
summary: Solution showing the Change class declaration with constructor, operator+, operator==, friend operator<<, private normalize(), and int q, d, p.
main_text: class Change { public: Change(int nq, int nd, int np); Change operator+(const Change& rhs) const; bool operator==(const Change& rhs) const; friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& ostr, const Change& c); private: void normalize(); int q, d, p; };. The class declaration shows: constructor taking initial quarter, dime, penny counts; operator+ as a const member function returning Change by value; operator== as a const member function returning bool; operator<< as a friend function (because ostream is the left operand, not Change); a private normalize() helper function; and three private int members for quarters, dimes, pennies.
notes_text: The design decisions here are instructive: operator+ and operator== are member functions because the left operand is a Change object. operator<< must be a friend non-member function because the left operand is ostream, not Change. normalize() is private because it is an implementation detail. Both operator+ and operator== are const because they don't modify the calling object.

title: Programming III Solution - Change Class Implementation
summary: Solution showing full implementation of Change constructor with normalize, normalize() using division/modulo, operator+, operator==, and operator<<.
main_text: Change::Change(int nq, int nd, int np) { q = nq; d = nd; p = np; normalize(); }. void Change::normalize() { int total = d*10 + p; q += total / 25; total = total % 25; d = total / 10; p = total % 10; }. Change Change::operator+(const Change& rhs) const { Change c(q + rhs.q, d + rhs.d, p + rhs.p); return c; }. bool Change::operator==(const Change& rhs) const { return (q == rhs.q && d == rhs.d && p == rhs.p); }. std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& ostr, const Change& c) { ostr << 'Q:' << c.q << ' D:' << c.d << ' P:' << c.p; return ostr; }. The normalize function converts dimes and pennies to total cents (d*10 + p), then distributes into quarters (total/25), remaining dimes (remainder/10), and remaining pennies (remainder%10). operator+ creates a new Change with summed values (constructor auto-normalizes). operator== compares all three fields. operator<< outputs in Q:x D:y P:z format.
notes_text: The elegance of this design is that normalization happens automatically in the constructor, so operator+ simply adds the raw values and lets the constructor normalize the result. operator== can directly compare q, d, p because normalization guarantees a unique canonical representation. The ostream operator returns ostr by reference to support chaining (cout << c1 << c2). Note that normalize only needs to convert dimes and pennies since quarters are already the largest denomination.
